United States Court of Appeals For the First Circuit No. 24-1286 MIYA WATER PROJECTS NETHERLANDS B.V., Plaintiff, Appellant, v. FINANCIAL OVERSIGHT AND MANAGEMENT BOARD FOR PUERTO RICO, Defendant, Appellee. APPEAL FROM THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE DISTRICT OF PUERTO RICO [Hon.
May 19, 2025 RIKELMAN, Circuit Judge. The Transparency and Expedited Procedure for Public Records Access Act (TEPPRA) creates a right to sue the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico to access public records and documents. See P.R. Laws Ann. tit. 3, § 9913 · (1) (2019). Appellant Miya Water Projects brought a claim under TEPPRA against the Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico ("the Board").
Miya also contends that, to the extent the Board shares Puerto Rico's Eleventh Amendment immunity, the Commonwealth waived that immunity through TEPPRA. We agree with the district court that Puerto Rico's Eleventh Amendment immunity extends to the Board and that the Commonwealth did not waive that immunity through TEPPRA.
If the government denies a person's records request, the statute empowers that person "to file, pro se or by counsel, a Special Petition for Public Records Disclosure Order with the Court of First Instance of the Judicial Region of his residence." Id. § 9919. In May 2022, Miya invoked TEPPRA to seek records from the Board about its cancellation of a water infrastructure project on which Miya had bid.

Binding precedent and Miya's own concessions settle most of the legal principles that resolve this appeal: Puerto Rico enjoys Eleventh Amendment immunity, the Board is an "arm" of Puerto Rico, and Congress did not abrogate the Board's Eleventh Amendment immunity through PROMESA.2 Indeed, by our assessment, the parties dispute only two issues. First, they disagree on whether a legal framework other than the arm-of-the-state test should determine whether Puerto Rico's Eleventh Amendment immunity extends to the Board. The First Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of a breach of contract claim brought by Miya Water Projects Netherlands B.V. against the Fund for the Office of the Secretary-General of the United Nations (FOMB). The court held that the contract was unenforceable because it was not properly ratified by the United Nations, which lacked the capacity to enter into such an agreement without proper authorization. The court also rejected Miya's arguments regarding apparent authority and estoppel, finding no evidence that the UN had held out the individuals who signed the contract as having the authority to bind it. The court held: The court held that a contract with the Fund for the Office of the Secretary-General of the United Nations (FOMB) was unenforceable because it was not properly ratified by the United Nations, as required by its internal regulations and the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.. The court found that the individuals who signed the contract on behalf of FOMB lacked the actual authority to bind the United Nations, and that Miya failed to demonstrate that the UN had clothed them with apparent authority.. The court rejected Miya's argument that the UN should be estopped from denying the contract's validity, as there was no evidence of misrepresentation or conduct by the UN that led Miya to reasonably believe the signatories had authority.. The court determined that the district court correctly applied the "act of state" doctrine by refusing to question the validity of the UN's internal decision-making processes regarding contract ratification.. The court affirmed the dismissal of Miya's breach of contract claim, concluding that no valid contract existed between Miya and FOMB due to the lack of proper authorization and ratification by the United Nations..

Miya sought access to public records related to a canceled water infrastructure project. The Board, established by Congress in 2016, refused to provide the requested documents, claiming TEPPRA did not apply to it. Miya then sued the Board in the United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico.

On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reviewed the district court's decision de novo. The appellate court agreed with the lower court's findings, holding that Puerto Rico's Eleventh Amendment immunity extends to the Board and that the Commonwealth did not waive this immunity through TEPPRA. The court emphasized that a waiver of Eleventh Amendment immunity must be unequivocally expressed in the statute's text, which TEPPRA did not do. Consequently, the appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Miya's claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.

ultimate.snippet: Miya Water Projects Netherlands B.V. v. FOMB, decided by First Circuit on May 19, 2025, resulted in a defendant win outcome. The First Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of a breach of contract claim brought by Miya Water Projects Netherlands B.V. against the Fund for the Office of the Secretary-General of the United Nations (FOMB). The court held that the contract was unenforceable because it was not properly ratified by the United Nations, which lacked the capacity to enter into such an agreement without proper authorization. The court also rejected Miya's arguments regarding apparent authority and estoppel, finding no evidence that the UN had held out the individuals who signed the contract as having the authority to bind it. The court held: The court held that a contract with the Fund for the Office of the Secretary-General of the United Nations (FOMB) was unenforceable because it was not properly ratified by the United Nations, as required by its internal regulations and the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.. The court found that the individuals who signed the contract on behalf of FOMB lacked the actual authority to bind the United Nations, and that Miya failed to demonstrate that the UN had clothed them with apparent authority.. The court rejected Miya's argument that the UN should be estopped from denying the contract's validity, as there was no evidence of misrepresentation or conduct by the UN that led Miya to reasonably believe the signatories had authority.. The court determined that the district court correctly applied the "act of state" doctrine by refusing to question the validity of the UN's internal decision-making processes regarding contract ratification.. The court affirmed the dismissal of Miya's breach of contract claim, concluding that no valid contract existed between Miya and FOMB due to the lack of proper authorization and ratification by the United Nations..
